items.title: F1 in Mexico City: Yet another Ferrari fiasco, but that’s not all
items.author: Jonathan M. Gitlin
items.content: Formula 1 has a new World Drivers' Champion. Just a few months after turning 20, Kimi Antonelli sealed his first title this weekend at Mexico City, becoming the sport’s youngest-ever champion. Elsewhere, there was drama aplenty, perhaps a consequence of the thin air affecting decision-making in some cases. The race was Ferrari’s to win, but yet again, the team handed victory to a rival this season, in this case Red Bull. Further down the grid, we saw a last-minute driver change in the Haas team, synchronized retirements from both Aston Martins, and the wheels literally coming off Cadillac Racing. And there was I, expecting a dull weekend. It might not be as high as Pikes Peak, but at an elevation of 7,350 feet (2,240 m) above sea level, the Autódromo Hermanos Rodríguez provides a unique challenge on the F1 calendar. Wings that would create huge amounts of downforce at circuits like Monaco just generate Monza-like levels in Mexico, and there’s little slipstream effect when following another car. Cooling tends to be a problem, too, with insufficient airflow across radiators, and obviously engine power is reduced with less oxygen to burn. The track is very flat, with a rather low-grip surface and mostly medium- and slow-speed corners, including a processional route through a stadium that was built in the 1990s, plus a very long run from the start into turn 1. items.title: Launch HN: Momentic (YC W24) – Agents that catch bugs by using your app
items.author: wuweiweiwu
items.content: Hey HN, we’re Wei-Wei and Jeff. We’re building Momentic, QA agents that autonomously plan, explore, and bug-bash controls and user flows in your web, iOS, Android, and (soon) desktop apps to catch bugs. Here’s a demo: https://youtu.be/BFsM-Se1Fh8 We’re both software engineers that spent our careers on dev tooling and infra across companies like Robinhood, Retool, WeWork, and Qualtrics. Testing was always a pain in the ass (esp Playwright and Selenium), so we built agents to do it for us. Modern day software has a ton of bugs and the change failure rate is only growing faster as coding agent adoption scales. LLMs are really good at generating code, but reinforce their own assumptions, write a ton of useless tests, and are bad at visual understanding. On DeepSWE v1.1, Sonnet 5.5 hit 66.2% pass rate when banned from writing tests, versus 65.3% when allowed. OSS end-to-end testing frameworks like Playwright, Selenium, or Maestro force you to hardcode implementation details like XPath, text, or aria-* attributes in your tests. Even with agents, these take a nontrivial amount of time and tokens to build and maintain. In 2023, we saw Nat Friedman drive a browser with GPT-3 via natbot. We were inspired to use this technology to automate the most painful and tedious parts of software engineering: testing. We started with using LLMs to generate and maintain Playwright, but quickly realized that those primitives were fundamentally misaligned with the agentic SDLC. We think the future of QA is agents testing themselves, not writing scripts. Mo is a custom agent harness for catching bugs that builds on the past 3 years of Momentic and millions of test traces from complex, real-world applications. Mo is built for recall: it finds the most real bugs, though Codex is a bit more precise at 86% vs 84%. The tradeoff is cost: Mo costs $2.67 per bug vs $0.80 for Codex, less than Claude Code and Devin. - Self-organizing agent graph. Mo builds a directed acyclic graph (DAG) as it explores. Large product areas automatically fork into parallel sub-agents, each with their own browser or device for concurrent execution. - Specialized agents for domain specific tasks. Planner agents reason over screenshots and video while dedicated locator agents inspect page structure to resolve plain-English interaction targets. Others include image analysis, video understanding, audio generation, and more. - Parallel agents coordinate through cooperative resource leases. Agents can announce that they’re “using” or “modifying” overlapping resources or fixtures. Multiple “using” claims can coexist, but only a single “modifying” claim can be active on any particular one. - Scaled infrastructure. Mo ships with a tunnel that lets users expose private sites and local apps to our hosted agents and infra. A single bug bash can spin up 100s of concurrent browsers and devices. We benchmarked Mo against coding agents on 4 popular open-source apps: Gitea (58.8k stars), Metabase, Twenty (YC), and Saleor, with 1,396 human-labeled bugs. Each agent got the same brief, a fresh E2B sandbox, and no access to source code. Codex and Claude Code used hosted Browserbase browsers, while Devin used its built-in browser. For evaluators, we implemented LLM as a judge (GPT-6.1 Sol) with a human reviewer. Results from a time-boxed 60-minute run: - Mo: 269 bugs, 19.3% recall, 84% precision, $2.67 per bug - Codex (GPT-6.1 Sol + Playwright MCP): 86 bugs, 6.2% recall, 86% precision, $0.80 per bug - Claude Code (Opus 5.5 + Playwright MCP): 59 bugs, 4.2% recall, 80% precision, $4.09 per bug - Devin: 27 bugs, 1.9% recall, 84% precision, $3.89 per bug Mo finds more bugs the more time it has. From 30 to 60 minutes, it went from 177 to 269 bugs (+52%), while Codex gained only 16%. Results: https://momentic.ai/qa-bench Write-up: https://momentic.ai/blog/qa-bench Dataset: https://huggingface.co/datasets/momentic/qa-bench Harness: https://github.com/momentic-ai/qa-bench We just shipped PR testing for Vercel and Cloudflare deploy previews and we’re giving every new signup $250 in Mo spend. Paid plans have higher infra capacity and included usage along with options to top up. We’d love for you to try it out and give us feedback. Feel free to comment here, we’ll be around all day!

items.title: Show HN: Subvocal – Talk to your computer without making noise
items.author: aarushyadav
items.content: Hi HN, we're Aarush and Arnav from The Subvocal Company (YC F26) (https://subvocal.company/). We’re building smart glasses that let you talk to your computer without talking out loud. You can mouth words silently and discreetly and the glasses decode them to text at the speed of speech. Here's a video of Dave from YC trying it out: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9QdX1eObVYI (Edit: you don't actually have to move your lips or even open your mouth for this to work! Since the RF can see inside your mouth the system can be fine tuned on "internal speech". This isn't the automatic tongue movements that occur when "thinking" words to yourself, but more like mouthing with your lips closed. It's a bit weird to do, but with practice, we have been able to get it down pretty well.) Arnav and I were studying CS at Georgia Tech at the beginning of the year, with no experience in silent speech or sensing. We were both AI-native builders and power users of Wispr Flow. What bugged us was not being able to use these tools in the library (or an office) or in public. At Stanford’s TreeHacks in February, we decided to build the most technically ridiculous thing we could think of. We’d read about AlterEgo, a silent speech system out of MIT’s Media Lab, and wanted to recreate it in 36 hours. We built a crude prototype, sticking EMG electrodes onto my face: https://drive.google.com/file/d/1mwhv5HZMz3UTevdrgwS5O7g2jWV... We got it to kind of work at a letter level in a very janky way. It wasn’t good enough to win the hackathon, but convinced us to go all in. The first time I typed a sentence without anyone noticing, I felt the magic of the technology. We quickly realized EMG (reading muscle electrical signals) wouldn’t work: - Signal changes due to sweat - Electrical interference - Placement variability - Most importantly, no one wants to stick electrodes onto their face!! So we switched to RF and built the glasses you see now. They emit radio waves, similar to Bluetooth, that pass through your face. As they cross the tongue, lips and soft palate, they’re modulated by silent mouthing. We train foundation models on this data to decode these perturbations to text. Despite prior academic research, getting this to work was a huge engineering challenge. First we built an extremely low noise RF sensing stack. Then we had to place antennas so their fields overlapped maximally with the articulators. Our first attempt on glasses failed completely, so we reverted to old habits and taped antennas on our face: https://drive.google.com/file/d/1ks0dS0eZiTV9EqSFsyB_w5BBjpc... Since taping antennas consistently in the same spot and angle was hard, we created this weird but effective head rig to hold them in place: https://drive.google.com/file/d/1rhzNFpdDzr7oHk0isFY70dkoV4C... This worked, but obviously wasn’t a product yet. So we worked deep in simulations to design glasses that could hold the antennas. That evolved into our design now, with antennas embedded within the frames. Once we established there was a signal, the next hurdle was cross-user generalization. Everyone’s facial anatomy, and hence RF signal patterns, are vastly different. We tried algorithmic workarounds but realized the only lever was to massively scale pretraining data. So that’s what we did. We set up booths in our office and paid people to read prompts wearing our glasses, to pretrain our models on. This produced a beautiful scaling curve, with errors falling quickly as we scaled our dataset and cross-user performance becoming genuinely compelling (as you see in the video above; Dave only had a short 20-sentence calibration). We always heard about building things from first principles but never understood it before this. We tried tackling it top down but completely failed. Only when we broke each component (the antenna, electronics, ML) down to its fundamentals to understand and optimize it did we get it to work really well. Over the next few months we’re continuing R&D to turn our prototype glasses into the slick product on our website and ship in Q1 2027. We’re also scaling up our dataset to improve performance on edge cases. For anyone who loves voice dictation but hates using it around people, we’ve opened preorders for our first batch of 500 units, with a $200 discount off the final price. Allocation is running out quickly, so get yours at https://subvocal.co/preorder!

XDA later independently verified that the new rule appears in version 2.1.314 of the Claude Code binary, which was released on October 30. items.title: Compute Crunch? Startups Aim to Financialize It
items.author: Madeline Renbarger
items.content: Can AI compute be traded like a commodity? A handful of startups, including a buzzy company called Ornn, are betting big on the concept as they work to create standardized pricing for GPU usage and connect buyers and sellers with commodities-style futures markets and brokerage services. Ornn, which helps route GPU capacity from neoclouds and data centers to startups that are willing to pay for short-term contracts, is now in the midst of a new triple-tranche funding round with a top valuation of around $1 billion, with Thrive Capital and General Catalyst in talks to participate, per sources familiar with the matter. Axios had earlier reported the round was in talks. The company raised a $33 million seed round led by a16z crypto back in June. Another player, Silicon Data, has launched an hourly rental price index for GPUs based on aggregate data from around 100 different sources. It aims to be a pure data play — it doesn’t get involved in brokering access — and raised a $30.5 million Series A in August from Valor Equity Partners and Atreides Management’s joint AI fund. Former FTX US president Brett Harrison is adding compute to his derivatives exchange, called Architect, and raised $35 million in funding last December. Yet another, Liquid Compute, raised a $15 million seed round in September from FirstMark and Chemistry and has applied to launch a US exchange for compute futures and options. Despite all the action, the sector faces plenty of challenges. Selling compute futures requires sign-off from financial regulators, which none of these companies have yet attained. CME Group plans to list futures tied to Silicon Data’s H100 and B200 GPU rental indexes on the New York Mercantile Exchange, and ICE plans to list contracts referencing Ornn’s Compute Price index, but they have yet to receive regulatory approval. CME had targeted October 5 as its start date, but that’s since been pushed back. Some of the newer players want to challenge the existing exchanges and become regulated venues themselves. The CFTC issued a public request for comment on compute futures that could interrogate the biggest question of all: whether compute is standardized, interchangeable, and liquid enough to support a futures market. Unlike, say, metals, GPUs depreciate rapidly as new chips hit the market, making financialization of them even trickier. Even if compute is fungible enough to be traded like a commodity and regulatory approvals are forthcoming, it’s not clear whether the shortage of compute that’s creating demand for these kinds of services is a permanent state of affairs or simply a transient phase. Two investors told Newcomer they had passed on deals in the space due to those concerns, Startup Scramble AI mania has left many startups in the tricky position of trying to compete with industry giants for access to the compute they need. That’s what’s driving the brokerage side of the emerging compute marketplaces. Read more

items.title: Most of our measures of a key cognitive process don't agree
items.author: John Timmer
items.content: It's widely acknowledged that it's nearly impossible to publish negative results in scientific journals. "We didn't see anything" is a much harder sell than finding that a hypothesis is clearly right. Findings of no effect tend to either be shuffled off to low-profile journals or left behind as unpublished lab lore. The high-profile journal Nature, however, made a notable exception this week, publishing a study that tells us that a bunch of methods we have been using to try to measure a key emotional ability don't seem to be measuring the same thing. The results mean that we don't have a good way to measure the impact of a concept that is the basis of a key method in therapy. Inconsistencies One of the most successful forms of therapy is cognitive behavioral therapy, or CBT. In part, CBT is based on getting people to step back and engage in "cognitive reappraisal." This requires people to think over a situation that has caused a negative emotional response and find ways to reinterpret it so that it has less impact on them. The ability to engage in this process has been linked to emotional resilience. Read full article Comments

items.title: Third person dies of bird flu since virus started jumping to livestock
items.author: Beth Mole
items.content: A person in Washington state has died from bird flu after exposure at an infected dairy farm, state health officials reported Sunday. It marks the third human bird flu death in the US since a strain of highly pathogenic (H5) avian influenza (HPAI) made the unprecedented jump from wild, migratory birds to dairy cows, which was first reported in the US in March 2024. The person who died was a Yakima County resident and was said to have had underlying health conditions, which could have made the person more vulnerable to the infection. On Friday, county officials reported that the person was severely ill and hospitalized. In the subsequent announcement of the person's death, officials said they would not be releasing further information about the person, including their name, gender, or age, out of respect for the family's privacy. "Our hearts go out to the individual's family and loved ones during this difficult time," Dave Atteberry, health officer for the Yakima Health District, said in a statement. "Avian influenza can cause severe illness, particularly among people who have underlying health conditions. While this is a serious and heartbreaking outcome, the risk to the general public remains low." Read full article Comments

items.title: Scott Alexander’s Against SURA Seems Deeply Confused
items.author: TheZvi
items.content: If you are helping build something that might kill everyone, maybe stop doing that. Ideally, when you do stop, tell everyone else to also stop building it. That is certainly the obvious, first-level thing to do. You need a damn good reason to decide that no, actually you should keep building the thing that might kill everyone. Scott Alexander is worried too many people are insisting upon this too loudly. He comes out against a strategy focused on getting people to stop. I disagree. I think many of the claims, arguments and rhetoric in Scott’s post are quite poor by the standards that Scott Alexander would apply to himself. Scott clearly continues to support advocacy for a global pause, or what he calls Plan A. His objection is to those advocating primarily or exclusively for SURA, which stands for ‘stop unilaterally and raise awareness.’ The practical differences here are smaller than they may at first appear. This post first lays out my understanding of Scott Alexander’s core claims, then gives my core reactions to those claims, then goes over various questions in detail along with gathering the resulting discussions. Table of Contents Scott Alexander’s Core Claims. My High Level Responses To Scott’s Core Claims. Briefly on Alignment. Probabilities and How They Work. Building a Thing That Might Kill Everyone is Deontologically Evil. People Quitting Major Labs While Raising Alarms Obviously Works. On AI Forecasting. Advancing Capabilities Burns Timeline. But China. Ethical People Can Disagree With You. There Are More Than Two Outcomes. Efforts Are Complementary, Not Mutually Exclusive. If Anyone Builds It, Everyone Dies. Vaniver is Not Convinced. There Is No Consensus That We Should Exclusively Focus on Plan A. It’s Not the Incentives, It’s You. Anthropic Is Not Optimally Pursuing These Plans. Against Against Sura. Scott Alexander’s Core Claims Scott Alexander writes Against SURA, or the strategy of calling upon nations and companies building superintelligence to stop building it and calling upon employees of those labs to quit, even without reciprocity. Here is his definition and coinage: I’ll lump these ideas together under the heading of “SURA” – the idea that the only ethical course is for people/companies/countries to Stop Unilaterally + Raise Awareness, with no plan for what happens if race dynamics continue anyway. I interpret the planks of SURA’s platform as: Individual alignment-pilled AI companies are morally obligated to stop unilaterally, regardless of whether they expect race dynamics to continue in their absence. Individual alignment-pilled employees at these companies should quit, regardless of whether they’re in capabilities or alignment roles, and regardless of whether they think their company is morally better than its competitors. Individual alignment-pilled countries (for example, a hypothetical future alignment-pilled US) should ban or heavily restrict AI progress unilaterally, regardless of whether they expect other countries (for example, China) to continue racing in their absence. I mostly avoid quoting directly from the OP, since most of you likely read it. Scott’s basic frame of the situation is that there are two classes of plan: Plan A, his combination of AI 2040’s Plans A/S/Other, are plans that involve working for a global pause in AI development. Plan C, his combination of everything else, is where we don’t do that. Scott’s core arguments are that (this is my ITT summary of Scott): Many actions that aim to help your chances of pulling off Plan A hurt your chances of survival if Plan A fails and you are forced back into Plan C. Plan C benefits from ‘alignment-pilling’ the companies, whereas Plan A benefits from raising mass awareness, educating politicians and getting verification tech. SURA is one of the actions that hurts Plan C. Plan A is first best, and we should try to do it, but it probably won’t happen, and a large portion of our victories come from executing Plan C. The correct and traditional strategy is to support Plan A while also preparing to execute Plan C as best we can. SURA, telling whoever listens to unilaterally stop, de facto torches our chances for execution of Plan C in order to maximize the chances of getting to try Plan A. SURA is an increasingly popular strategy, but it only makes sense if you believe some combination of assumptions. Alignment is highly doomed, or is highly doomed under Plan C conditions. Racing to superintelligence under these conditions is deontologically evil. Racing burns valuable time. People quitting is helpful in raising awareness and pursuing a pause. SURA is actually bad for even your chances of getting Plan A. There is currently a ‘consensus in favor of SURA’ in rationalist/EA spaces. Scott also makes other claims, such as his overview of alignment. In many cases the claims seem overgeneralized or overstated. I respond to Scott’s claims, and without any implicit endorsement of claims I do not mention. My High Level Responses To Scott’s Core Claims True in general, but often false for specific actions where it is claimed. These actions all help both Plan A and Plan C, although they differentially help their respective plans more. If fully executed, yes. On the margin, the sign of impact is not obvious. True, given our uncertainty over the situation. I agree with Scott Alexander that this is his strongest point. There are those who disagree, and I respect the opposite position. True for the world overall, in aggregate. Not obviously true for an individual or group, and not obviously true on the margin. Extreme forms of SURA can be negative for Plan C, but on net and on the margin while sign is unclear I expect reasonable ones to be positive even for Plan C. These are key arguments in favor of SURA, but even if all four were false it would not definitively render SURA a bad idea, as this is not an exhaustive list. I have high model uncertainty on this. I respect those who think alignment under Plan C is highly doomed. They have good arguments. I am not fully convinced. Alignment under Plan C could turn out to be highly doomed, or building superintelligence could be highly doomed even if alignment is solved, or it is possible that alignment is ‘super doable’ although difficult. I am not a deontologist, but yeah, it seems rather deontologically evil. You might want to do it anyway, and at some point in a cost-benefit analysis you have to be willing to as Rao says Be Slightly Evil, but don’t pretend otherwise. Scott’s attempt to draw a parallel to frontier AI use feels very confused here. Obviously we don’t want to go full Asymmetric Justice. I’m pretty appalled by trying to say that actively working to develop the thing that might kill everyone is the same thing as the marginal economic impact of personal use of frontier models. This is just the ‘if I don’t do the evil thing, someone else will, so it’s fine to do it’ argument and I fully reject it. This seems obviously true to some extent. But we can talk price, both in terms of how much time and how valuable is that time. This again seems obviously true to me and we should be talking price. False in expectation on the margin for Plan A, arguably for Plan C as well per #4. False. There is not a consensus on this question. Even a weak version of this (with some amount of fallback) is a minority position, and the full version is rare. Briefly on Alignment It is not Scott’s main point, but I want to flag that I strongly disagree with Scott’s stated model of alignment. I do not believe that AI models are well-modeled as ‘inheriting virtue’ simply because they learn to imitate humans. If nothing else, this implies that AI base models are “virtuous” until you “corrupt” them with RLVR. No. This is at best highly misleading. This was a plausible candidate for the worst thing in the post. I do agree with Scott’s general theory of what Plan C alignment success looks like, in that it involves trying to string prosaic stopgaps together long enough to let the AI pivot to doing our alignment homework for us, and hopefully its alignment can become self-reinforcing and antifragile. I agree that this seems potentially possible, but I also think it is very easy to see multiple places where a p(doom) of 90%+ could come from, including: Even if we do ‘solve alignment’ our current plans on what to do with the resulting AIs would still doom us, and we can’t even properly discuss this in public, so it seems highly likely we will turn the world state unwinnable anyway, and die. Even if we can ‘solve alignment’ with strong implementation of prosaic alignment strategies leading to automated alignment research, the current quality of play inside the labs says we would very likely fail to execute on this anyway, and die. We are highly uncertain that the above prosaic strategy is viable even if done well. The most obvious and common reason for a very high p(doom) is to believe, in the style of Eliezer Yudkowsky, that alignment requires you to hit a very precise target, on the first try, while dodging a rather large List of Lethalities. They argue that asking AIs to automate the alignment research will inevitably mean they miss key elements or otherwise fail. I think that is super reasonable, and it is strange to me that Scott Alexander finds this hard to understand. Probabilities and How They Work This exchange has some abridged responses. Oliver Habryka: But yeah, I think you should obviously be willing to risk war if a foreign lab is working towards building ASI. Scott Alexander: I think these considerations apply in a small fraction of worlds where the US government is very alignment-pilled but China isn’t. … Under my model a really good Plan C+ has an 90%+ chance of working. Oliver Habryka: God man, I really find it extremely wild to think that we will solve the alignment problem with an expected 6-12 month lead, in a unilateral fashion and thereafter declare the end of history. This just seems so incredibly wild to me, and you are pursuing a strategy where you and your friends are building the machine gods unilaterally betting all you have on it. Scott Alexander: My reasoning in coming up with that number was that my unconditional p(doom) is 25%, and since a really good Plan C+ is a much better world than I expect in real life, it’s probably a little less than half that. Oliver Habryka: You don’t need to be “entirely united around solving the alignment problem” in order to think it’s a bad idea to build god-like machine intelligence. This is the whole central point I keep making. Countries have lots of reasons to think that it’s super bad news for other countries to go and build very powerful AI systems. The default outcome is that countries will try to prevent other countries from doing that, using existing tools of international diplomacy and escalation (and probably also using new AI technologies themselves). The level of buy-in necessary to start telling other countries to not do fucking crazy stuff is vastly vastly less than the level of buy-in necessary to “be entirely united around solving the alignment problem”. Indeed, I have trouble seeing a world where you don’t get enormous buy-in in basically every country in the world as military applications of AI start being widespread. [Thread continues.] You don’t get to start out with an unconditional p(doom) at the bottom of the page and then reason from that, or all you are doing is restating the 25%. At best this is an intuition pump. Also I find the idea that AI goes well 90% of the time on a C+ style plan to be pretty absurdist. There are multiple distinct steps that seem much more likely than this to go wrong under such conditions. This 90% is also 30%+ above every source Scott cites on this question. I mean, yes, obviously if you think that a prosaic and time pressured but reasonably executed plan has a 90%+ chance of success, then given the current state of the world your primary strategy should be to try and navigate to such a scenario. I would love, love, love to lock in a 90% success rate. Obviously that is an ‘unacceptable risk’ but there is no better alternative on offer. Scott is not actually advocating for full abandonment of Plan A in favor of Plan C, only coming out against those who would abandon Plan C for Plan A, which to me represents a substantially lower probability of success than 90% for a Plan C+. Building a Thing That Might Kill Everyone is Deontologically Evil If you believe there is no deontological prohibition against building a thing that might kill everyone, you don’t believe in deontological prohibitions. Which is fine. You can decide not to believe in them. But then say that. One can also say that there are times when you must do deontologically evil things in the service of a greater good, despite them being deontologically evil. Again, this is fine, and I even agree with you. But then say that. The same applies to virtue ethics arguments, which look similar in such cases. Certainly one must do some things that contribute to some other bad things. This is especially true if one counts engagement in trade that indirectly rewards efforts that also point towards other bad outcomes, despite the product you buy itself being good and causing good outcomes, or your actions incidentally providing tiny marginal funding for things that already have vast funding. One cannot go around never doing anything that is at all entangled with things that have negative consequences. One cannot count only the negative consequences of one’s actions, including indirect ones, and ignore the positive. That’s Asymmetric Justice, as I discussed in 2019, and it is incompatible with survival or civilization. There must exist ethical consumption under capitalism and also under other systems, especially consumption that enables your productivity in good causes. Ultimately one must talk price. I can see drawing a line that says, if your effort is sufficiently better than its rivals, or you are working on making that effort better, that it is correct to do the deontologically evil thing here and work on it anyway. I can also see drawing a line that says it is not ethical to use the products of such companies, or to own stock in Nvidia or Google. I declined to invest directly into Anthropic for ethical reasons, despite what I thought were excellent expected returns. Wherever one draws the line, one can see the ocean of difference between ‘buys a highly useful subscription to an existing AI service’ or ‘owns stock in tech companies’ versus ‘actively working on advancing capabilities inside a frontier lab.’ AdamYedidia: This post makes plenty of good points, but I think your argument against racing to superintelligence being deontologically evil is weak. Roughly speaking, you draw an analogy between developing AI and using AI as a consumer. There’s a few things I could say about that analogy directly: -The first is that the analogy has some merit, and that I don’t really feel amazing about my own heavy AI use. And I have at least one friend who has never used an LLM, explicitly because he doesn’t want to contribute in any way to the race to superintelligence and human extinction. Maybe some people would call his choice foolish, but I have a lot of respect for it. -The second thing is that there’s billions of users of AI, but only thousands/maybe tens of thousands of frontier AI developers. It makes a lot more sense to try to coordinate some kind of prohibition at the latter level and than at the former. And independent of the mechanics of a boycott, I think everyone has a reasonable understanding that the developers of AI bear a lot more individual responsibility for outcomes around AI than consumers do. But mostly, I think this deontological prohibition thing deserves more of your attention than you currently seem to be interested in giving it. There’s a lot to be said about the merits of deontology vs consequentialism and how they might apply to a situation like this one, but one thing I want to focus on in particular is that deontology is “normie ethics,” and when you’re considering doing something that will affect everyone, including every normie, it’s important to take into account how they will see it. The analogy I’d choose is driving. It’s hard to define exactly what it means to be a good or bad driver, but at least as important as raw skill is predictability, by which I mean how predictable you are to everyone else. If you drive 30 above the speed limit on the highway, weaving between lanes to pass the other cars, is that fine so long as you are skilled enough to avoid an accident? Is it fine to run a red light at night when there’s no one else around? Maybe it is, I guess. But I’d point out that that kind of strategy is brittle. It makes you unpredictable to everyone else. If something unexpected (to you) happens, your strategy fails catastrophically. In the same way, I think normies are baffled, confused, and repulsed by the thing where Anthropic employees, despite having p(doom)s, continue working on the tech anyway. The most common sentiment I hear, once I’ve fully explained the situation and insisted that no, it’s not them hyping, it’s not about the IPO, this is something they really truly believe, is “those people should be arrested.” I want to be very clear: I don’t agree that Anthropic employees should be arrested. I’m not even sure they’re doing the wrong thing. … In your open letter to Steven Pinker, you wrote: When Anthropic decided that the best way to forestall the AI apocalypse was to make a desperate push beyond the existing scientific frontier and create the dangerous AI themselves so they could be sure to get the technology right, with limitless benefits for humanity if they succeeded, you … played it for laughs, asking tongue-in-cheek “Why are the same people who warn that a technology will kill us all building it as fast as they can?” I saw that this particular passage of your post was making the rounds on X among people hostile to you and the cause of EA/AI safety in general. Generally people would quote it and say something like, “Look how crazy they are. Look at the the degree to which Scott has drunk the Kool-Aid. This is self-evidently insane.” Again: I don’t agree. I understand where Anthropic is coming from. I don’t think these Twitter dunks were in good faith. But: there’s a reason that passage in particular was chosen by your opponents as the part of the post that would make you look craziest. And it made you look crazy because, to most people, Anthropic’s entire strategy, its entire raison d’etre, looks crazy. Richard Ngo: Is there any part of this post that’s significant evidence against it being written as a knee-jerk defense of Anthropic? To be clear, I am open to people honestly evaluating ways in which Anthropic is or isn’t trustworthy, and then coming down in defense of them. But I model Scott as being committed to defending Anthropic on an emotional level. Oliver Habryka: I think Scott’s strategy violates various deontological and virtue-ethical principles that are very different (which of course I support adopting because doing so makes the world better on-net, but my relationship to them is very different than naive consequentialist-type arguments). I think Scott has a weak argument that my strategy is violating important deontological and virtue-ethical principles, and this makes this a real asymmetry. Of course, which deontological and virtue-ethical principles are the right ones to adopt is most of what ethics is about, but I dispute the frame that there is some simple gotcha here. People Quitting Major Labs While Raising Alarms Obviously Works The evidence of this seems overwhelming to me in the wake of Jacob Coxon, even more so than it already was after others including Daniel Kokotajlo. The public debate has been radically changed by such voices, from people who had little effective voice when they were inside the labs. Scott Alexander acknowledges that Coxon’s resignation did a lot of good, for both Plan A and Plan C, but says this is only because he worked for Anthropic in particular, and because Evan Hubinger stayed and confirmed his claims. I agree that these were contributing factors to the magnitude of impact, but we have had a number of impactful other resignations, often from OpenAI. That does not mean that any given person obviously gets more leverage from exit than they do from voice. You can absolutely make a case that staying on the inside and working to improve lab policies or even to differentially favor one lab is more valuable a task for you in particular, or that the overall solution is a mixed strategy. Daniel Kokotajlo: Similarly, I think that individuals quitting the big AI companies is not necessarily the best thing they could do. Being very vocal publicly about the dangers while advocating strongly for change internally, until you get fired, seems like it could be even better. However, I think quitting and speaking up is an excellent baseline to compare strategies against, and historically it seems like most full-time-safety people inside the companies have failed to beat this baseline. (And it’s even more clear for the full-time-capabilities people.) And the reason they have failed to beat this baseline is that they have convinced themselves that they are pursuing a more sophisticated and effective strategy of achieving change on the inside and putting themselves in a good position for later etc. I want to throw cold water in their faces and get them to think more clearly about whether what they are doing really is better than the baseline or not. I do know that there are a number of people who, despite being relatively high up in their organizations, still felt like they had little effective voice. This includes Joshua Achiam, Miles Brundage and Steven Adler. We have a lot of evidence that internally advocating for safety is difficult, and also that if you do so and then get fired this can be a lot less impactful than if you quit. See Jasmine Wang, Tomek Korbak and Mikita Balesni, whether or not they were fired for good cause. Scott Alexander then doubles down in his second section. Here I find this absurd. Scott Alexander: The key demand of SURA is that alignment-pilled people and companies stop unilaterally. The likely end result is that we only have non-alignment-pilled companies, staffed entirely by non-alignment-pilled employees, left in the AI industry. But the presence of alignment-pilled companies is one of the strongest levers that we have to change the political situation and enact a global pause. Eliminating them makes it harder to win political fights, convince the masses, and convince China. I do not understand how you can think, after everything that has happened, that this is true. Loud resignations have very obviously made it easier to win political fights both inside and outside the labs. They have directly convinced the masses. My steelman of Scott’s argument in sections II.A and II.B is to assume he is ignoring the margin, and only talking about an extreme scenario where many or most lab employees who care about safety quit, shifting the balance of power in the labs towards those who do not care. I agree that narrowly, in terms of motivating action inside the labs, a sufficient number of worried people quitting would start to substantially tip their actions, and this would plausibly outweigh the signaling and other effects. But we are orders of magnitude from that point, our efforts on the margin are not going to get us to that point, and before we reached that point the labs would likely be crippled by lack of ability to do good technical safety work. On AI Forecasting Scott Alexander several times refers to ‘AI superforecaster’ predictions. It seems reasonable to use AI forecasting as a sanity check or additional data point. For things where traditional ‘superforecasters’ or others following similar protocols have a strong track record, we should be using AI forecasting, and also human superforecasting, more often. However, when it comes to core developments in AI, superforecasters have an atrocious track record, and AI forecasts also have an atrocious track record, and I do not think this was bad luck. I think that scenarios like this break the types of heuristics and pattern matching that have traditionally been rewarded in such places. A simple test, before asking things like ‘does it make sense that Anthropic disbanding their entire company would only raise the chance of a global pause from 16% to 19%’ is to ask whether this system makes reasonable predictions for other aspects of AI, and whether it assigned (for example) extremely tiny probabilities to various AI breakthroughs that have happened in 2026. Another is to use common sense. I can totally see an argument that Anthropic disbanding to raise awareness would only raise chances by 3%, if you think pauses are extremely unlikely – say, from 2% to 5%. In which case, such a move seems clearly foolish. But if you think there is already a 16% chance, then my brain does not find it plausible that incinerating a $1.5+ trillion company, which would be the costliest signal in human history, would only raise this chance to 19%. Daniel Kokotajlo: I think the positive effects of a single frontier US company stopping unilaterally are larger than you or the AI forecaster think. I think that the discourse would be massively changed overnight if there was such a giant costly signal that the company actually was terrified of the risks. TsviBT: The presumptive fact that there’s a grossly insufficient amount of serious effort towards a global stop coming from Anthropic, implies that so far all the hundreds or thousands of people who were conflicted about joining, and then joined, haven’t caused a non-grossly-insufficient effort. This is a strong argument against the value of joining. Against Against Sura For the purposes of discussing what to do next, let us break up SURA into Absurd SURA, Strong SURA and Weak SURA, and then there is non-SURA. Absurd SURA says the only ethical or valid action is to tell countries to ban AI capabilities development, labs to shut down and employees to quit. I call it ‘Absurd SURA’ because this is an obviously dumb strawman. Disregard. Strong SURA says the only ethical or valid action is to stop developing AI capabilities. Ideally one would coordinate with other nations or labs to do so. But, failing that, nations must ban AI capabilities development, labs must shut down and employees must quit. It is not worth investing in a fallback plan, and indeed it is at least arguably better not to help the labs with their prosaic alignment as this prevents warning shots. I think this is a valid position to take. It is right if one believes that prosaic alignment plans as could potentially be implemented by Anthropic or OpenAI are doomed. As in, if you think that a realistic ‘Plan C+’ very likely causes everyone to die. Weak SURA says that you should fight hard for Plan A and for a coordinated pause, that on the margin more employees should loudly quit, and that if coordination is unsuccessful then labs and nations should soon point pause even on their own, if capabilities advance the way the labs predict they will advance. But that a better execution of Plan C can matter a lot too, so you should also simultaneously strive to maximize our chances of a good execution of Plan C. Non-SURA is opposed even to Weak SURA, and prefers to optimize Plan C. It tries to back ‘the good guys’ which typically means America and Anthropic, and to ensure they have as big a lead as possible. Scott Alexander spends his post arguing against at least Strong SURA. My position on this is that I respect advocates of Strong SURA, I am walking the path of Weak SURA, and I reject both Absurd SURA and non-SURA. Should you treat lab employees as deontologically evil people? I say no. Nor do you need to shun or be rude to them. But I do think you should treat them, whether or not they have good reason to do it, as participating in a deontologically evil thing. When you are building a thing that might kill everyone there might be no better play available, but also you should seriously consider maybe not doing that.

items.title: Building AI for Lawyers - Jacob Lauritzen, CTO of Legora
items.author: Basil Chatha
items.content: In this episode, we chat with Jacob Lauritzen, CTO of Legora, following the announcement of their $550M Series E at an $8.8B valuation a couple weeks ago. We talk about what it takes to build AI agents for lawyers and what other people building agents can learn from that work. Legora started in a Stockholm basement with a simple product: ChatGPT, Swedish law, and a search tool. Jacob had already been through YC with his own startup when he helped Max Junestrand with the application for Leya (now Legora). He later joined as head of engineering and is now CTO. Today the agent drafts and edits Word documents, reviews thousands of contracts at once, and coordinates work between lawyers, their clients, and other agents. The company passed $100 million in ARR in April, less than 18 months after launch, and now has more than 1,800 customers. It raised $550 million in March at a $5.55 billion valuation, then another $550 million in October at an $8.8 billion valuation. Its latest acquisition, Wexler, was its fifth just this year. We asked Jacob how you evaluate agents when you can't see your customers' data, which tasks still need better models, how legal engineers and forward deployed engineers split the work, and why the billable hour as a business model is being upended. Watch the full conversation on YouTube → Open video on YouTube ↗ What changed for the billable hour? When Jacob first read Leya's YC application, he had one piece of feedback: people had tried building legal tech a million times, and it never worked. If lawyers bill by the hour, getting faster means earning less. Why would they buy a tool that does that? What changed, he says, is the pressure on firms. In the US, routine work like small reviews is already shifting to flat project fees. Some firms do it for free to hold on to the client. The money moves to M&A, litigation, and time spent with clients. We asked whether that means firms will stop needing paralegals and junior lawyers. Jacob says that's not what Legora is seeing. A good junior is worth more today than two years ago because they get so much more done, just as in engineering. Jump to the billing model discussion → Evals without access to customer data Most teams improve their agents by reading traces. Legora can't read any. Almost everything users upload is confidential, and much of it belongs to the firm's clients, not the firm. So the evals team has to recreate the kinds of work customers do. Three engineers and three lawyers build RL environments to simulate the work their customers do. One example is a 10,000-file data room where the agent runs due diligence and has to produce a report that catches the right red flags. The team plots the results on a heat map by practice area and task. A new model often gets better at some kinds of legal work and worse at others. The team draws on a pool of about 100 legal engineers: lawyers who spent three or four years in big law, often with a CS degree. In production, Legora classifies failures into 10 to 20 known failure modes and runs cheap LLM-based checks behind feature flags. Those restrictions also determine which infrastructure Legora can use. Everything runs on Azure because when Legora started, law firms wouldn't accept AWS or GCP, and Microsoft was already an approved vendor through 365. Jump to evals without traces → Where smarter models still matter Legora resisted a model picker for a long time before giving in. Jacob's view is that a lawyer shouldn't have to decide whether a contract is a Sonnet-high or an Opus-mid task. It's Legora's job to find the best available tradeoff between quality, cost, latency, governance, and regional availability. He estimates that models already handle about 60% of legal work really well. For those tasks it's a cost and latency problem now. Complex analysis and editing across million-token contracts still need more intelligence. Legora has started post-training open-weight models for narrow tasks like legal research, with no plans to train its own frontier model. For drafting, Jacob finds Fable and Opus too verbose. Astra is more concise. To address hallucinations, everything the agent writes gets a citation that highlights a bounding box in the source PDF, multiple layers down. Jump to the model discussion → A few building blocks, many products Six months into the job, Jacob showed the team a slide of the 300 Spartans and declared that Legora would stay at 20 engineers forever. It now has 100, and he says that still feels too small. His job now is to build a system where the team can ship just a few things and customers feel like they're getting a lot. The team builds around a few primitives: projects that hold files, the agent, Tabular Review, and lists. Lists are a flexible Notion-style database with triggers and automations. Agents can create and read lists, and changes to a list can start an agent. Intake is a Slack bot that turns a request into a ticket on a list. Tabular Review is the one the industry copied, down to the name. Each row is a document, each column is a question. Drop in 10,000 employment contracts and ask for the termination period, the IP assignment clause, and the severance terms. It supports up to a million cells, but starts with just 10 rows so you can fix your prompts before running the rest. Legal engineers configure new products on these primitives without writing code. Even Wexler's fact intelligence product runs on the same building blocks. Jump to the primitives discussion → Legal engineers first, forward deployed engineers second Legora hired its first forward deployed engineer about nine months ago in New York: Di Qi, a two-time YC founder who worked on search at Meta. Legal engineers configure the product the way a power user would and don't write code. Forward deployed engineers write code into production, build integrations into a firm's CRM or document management system, and push what they learn back into the core product. They still don't touch client data. When a big, engaged client signs, Legora assigns legal engineers to work with them and adds an FDE if the project needs one. Within a year, Jacob expects to have a rotating group of FDEs who sit with a client for a couple of months, build what they need, and move on. Jump to the forward deployed discussion → Where this goes In two years, Jacob thinks big enterprises will use Legora through tools like Claude Cowork, while law firms work inside Legora directly. He doesn't expect the labs to cut Legora off the way they've done to coding companies. For a $400 million M&A deal, he thinks people will still want Legora. Jump to the predictions → Show notes Legora — the collaborative AI platform for lawyers, where Jacob is CTO. Jacob Lauritzen — Jacob on LinkedIn. Legora's Series E announcement — $550 million at an $8.8 billion valuation, with ARR above $200 million. "Agents need more than a chat" — Jacob's talk at AI Engineer Europe 2026. "Connect AI to Billions of Legal Documents" — Jacob's AI Engineer talk with Simon Eskildsen of turbopuffer. How Legora runs 2,000 parallel agent evals on Modal Sandboxes — the infrastructure behind Legora's eval runs. Legora acquires Qura — the Stockholm legal research startup Legora bought in April. Legora is acquiring Wexler — the London startup that extracts and verifies facts across large litigation document sets.
